lessons.title: Know the Main Coating Types
lessons.objective: Distinguish paint, primer, stain, and clear finishes.
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers may call every can of coating “paint.” The right product depends on the surface and the desired result.

content.heading: Paint and primer
content.text: Paint adds color and a protective finish. Primer prepares certain surfaces for a topcoat. Some paints advertise built-in priming features, but that does not mean they replace a separate primer in every situation.

content.heading: Stain and clear finishes
content.text: Stain changes the appearance of wood while allowing some grain to show. Clear finishes protect or change the sheen without adding an opaque color. Products vary by intended surface and exposure.

content.heading: Start with the project
content.text: Ask what the customer is coating, whether it is indoors or outdoors, and whether the existing surface is bare, painted, or stained. Read the product label before recommending a category.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for “paint” to keep a new wooden bench looking natural. A clear exterior-rated finish or appropriate stain may be closer to the goal than opaque wall paint.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “Do you want to see the wood grain, or cover it with color?” Then compare only products labeled for that surface and use.
lessons.common_mistakes: Treating primer as a finish coat; assuming every clear finish works outdoors.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a paint specialist when the surface or previous coating is unknown, or when product labels conflict.

unscored_practice.question: Which product category is most likely to preserve visible wood grain?

choices.text: Wood stain or a suitable clear finish

unscored_practice.explanation: A stain or clear finish can preserve the appearance of wood grain. The exact product must be suitable for the project.

lessons.title: Choose Interior or Exterior Products
lessons.objective: Identify location and exposure before choosing paint.
lessons.why_this_matters: Products designed for one setting may not be appropriate for another.

content.heading: Location comes first
content.text: Ask whether the surface is indoors, outdoors, or in a special setting such as a porch floor. A covered porch still has temperature and moisture exposure.

content.heading: Exposure matters
content.text: Sunlight, moisture, foot traffic, and frequent cleaning affect the product choice. A wall coating and a floor coating are not interchangeable.

content.heading: Use label language
content.text: Look for the approved surfaces and uses on the label. Never promise weather resistance, washability, or durability beyond the product instructions.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants leftover interior wall paint for outdoor shutters. You explain that exterior exposure calls for a coating labeled for that use.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “Where is the surface, and what will it be exposed to?” Show the intended-use section on the can.
lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming all paint works on all surfaces; treating a covered outdoor space as indoor.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate unusual substrates, high moisture, or coatings with special handling instructions.

lessons.title: Understand Paint Sheen
lessons.objective: Explain common sheen choices without making absolute promises.
lessons.why_this_matters: Sheen changes how a painted surface looks and how visible surface flaws may appear.

content.heading: Sheen is the finish appearance
content.text: Flat and matte finishes reflect less light. Eggshell and satin show more reflection. Semi-gloss and gloss reflect more light.

content.heading: Compare tradeoffs
content.text: Higher-sheen finishes may make surface imperfections more noticeable. Cleaning performance varies by product formulation, not just sheen.

content.heading: Match the room and preference
content.text: Ask about lighting, surface condition, traffic, and desired look. Use the actual product sample and label rather than assuming every brand performs alike.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a low-shine bedroom wall but also asks about cleaning marks. You compare the manufacturer’s available finishes and washability information.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s compare the look and the cleaning claims on these two specific products.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Claiming that every satin paint is washable; recommending gloss without asking about wall condition.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Seek help if a customer needs specialized scrubbability, commercial, or moisture-performance claims.

lessons.title: Read the Paint Can
lessons.objective: Find the label details that guide a safe recommendation.
lessons.why_this_matters: A product label is more reliable than memory when requirements vary.

content.heading: Look for intended surfaces
content.text: Check approved substrates, interior or exterior use, and any exclusions.

content.heading: Find preparation and application directions
content.text: Labels may specify cleaning, sanding, priming, application temperature, dry time, recoat time, and ventilation. Follow the specific product instructions.

content.heading: Know the difference between dry and recoat
content.text: Dry-to-touch does not necessarily mean ready for another coat, washing, or heavy use. Explain the exact label timing.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants to repaint a table tonight and use it tomorrow morning. You check the label for recoat and return-to-service guidance instead of guessing.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Point to the label section that supports your answer. If the directions are unclear, consult the manufacturer’s technical data.
lessons.common_mistakes: Making up cure times; overlooking ventilation and surface restrictions.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate questions about hazardous coatings, old coatings of unknown origin, or unusual application conditions.

lessons.title: Ask the Right Paint Questions
lessons.objective: Use a short consultation to narrow the options.
lessons.why_this_matters: A few clear questions prevent a wrong purchase and unnecessary returns.

content.heading: Five questions
content.text: Ask: What surface? Indoors or outdoors? Existing finish and condition? Desired appearance? How will the surface be used?

content.heading: Do not skip preparation
content.text: Peeling paint, dirt, grease, and damp surfaces can affect results. Customers may need cleaning, repairs, or a separate primer.

content.heading: Confirm before checkout
content.text: Repeat the project and product choice. Identify supplies that are genuinely needed, without pressuring the customer.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer says, “I need a gallon of white paint.” You learn it is for a stained exterior railing and pause to check preparation and product compatibility.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Before we choose the can, can I ask what you are painting and what is on it now?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Selecting only by color; assuming the customer knows the existing finish.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask for assistance with lead-paint concerns, mold, major moisture problems, or unfamiliar coating systems.
